description: We are a team formed by current students and professionals coders that are interested in creating new innovative software and hardware.
summary:
ASTRA-MED AI is our prototype for keeping astronaut health information useful, even when communication with Earth is unreliable.

We developed two connected medical dashboards: one for astronauts aboard a spacecraft and another for doctors on Earth.

Our system simulates wearable biometric sensors that continuously monitor heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), respiratory rate and skin temperature. It records measurements, displays changing health trends, identifies readings that need attention and provides AI-assisted medical summaries.

One of our key features is communication resilience. When the simulated connection to Earth is lost, onboard monitoring continues and new measurements are saved. Once communication returns, the stored information can synchronize with Earth.

We also integrated 164 historical NASA RadLab radiation readings alongside our simulated astronaut data.

Our goal is to explore how astronauts could monitor their health more independently during long-duration space missions. ASTRA-MED is a nonclinical prototype, not a certified medical system.
details:
Why we built ASTRA-MED

During long-duration space missions, astronauts cannot always depend on immediate medical assistance from Earth. Communication delays or temporary disconnections can make sharing important health information difficult.

We wanted to explore how software could help astronauts understand changes in their health while keeping doctors on Earth informed whenever communication is available.

How our system works

ASTRA-MED has two main interfaces.

The Spacecraft Medical Station allows astronauts to view their biometric measurements, monitor health trends, record symptoms and review medical alerts.

The Earth Medical Control dashboard allows medical personnel to monitor synchronized astronaut information, review historical measurements and record medical observations.

To demonstrate continuous monitoring, we created a simulated wearable sensor system. It generates changing biometric measurements for four fictional astronauts using individual baseline profiles and activity-dependent variations.

Every observation is recorded with its value, unit, timestamp and source, allowing users to examine historical trends and identify unusual changes.

AI-assisted health monitoring

ASTRA-MED includes a medical summary assistant that helps users understand their measurements.

Instead of displaying only raw data, the assistant organizes information into readable summaries, findings, warnings and supporting evidence.

Our system supports configurable cloud AI assistance and a deterministic rule-based fallback. These features help explain observations but are not intended to replace medical professionals or make independent diagnoses.

Communication blackout simulation

One of our main features is the ability to simulate communication loss between a spacecraft and Earth.

Using the Mission Link control, we can disable communication while keeping onboard health monitoring operational.

During the blackout, new measurements continue being recorded and outgoing information is queued.

When the connection is restored, pending observations can synchronize with the Earth monitoring system.

This demonstrates how medical data could be preserved during interruptions in future space missions.

NASA data integration

We integrated 164 historical radiation measurements from NASA's Open Science Data Repository RadLab.

The application displays radiation measurements with their original timestamps, instruments and scientific units.

This data is kept separate from our synthetic astronaut measurements because historical radiation observations do not represent live personal exposure.

Real vs. Simulated Data

ASTRA-MED is a fully functional software prototype, but almost all the medical data displayed in the application is simulated.

Our four astronauts are fictional, and their biometric measurements—including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), respiratory rate, blood pressure, skin temperature, sleep patterns, and activity levels—are synthetically generated to demonstrate how the monitoring system works.

Medical alerts, symptoms, patient histories, and demonstration scenarios are also based on fictional data. These measurements are designed to behave realistically but do not come from actual astronauts or medical devices.

The only real scientific measurement dataset integrated into our project is NASA's RadLab radiation dataset, containing 164 historical radiation observations.

We clearly separate these authentic NASA measurements from our simulated astronaut health data.

Although the medical data is synthetic, the dashboards, monitoring logic, data recording, AI-assisted summaries, and communication synchronization are implemented as working software features.

Our project demonstrates the technology's potential rather than claiming to provide clinically validated medical monitoring.

Technologies used

We developed the interfaces using Angular, TypeScript, HTML and CSS.

Our application logic uses NestJS and Node.js to handle health observations, authentication, data processing and communication between the two systems.

We also use persistent data storage, JSON datasets and tools for presenting biometric trends.

ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex assisted our team during planning, coding, debugging and interface development.

What makes ASTRA-MED different

Our focus is not simply collecting measurements. We wanted to make health information understandable, traceable and available even when communication is interrupted.

By combining simulated monitoring, historical records, evidence-linked medical summaries and delayed synchronization, ASTRA-MED demonstrates a possible approach to more independent astronaut health monitoring.

The project uses synthetic astronaut data and has not been clinically validated or connected to operational spacecraft medical equipment.
